---
title: "Markov chain Monte Carlo"
---

[Monte Carlo integration](monte-carlo-integration.qmd) used independent draws from a target distribution. Direct posterior draws are often unavailable. [**Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)**](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/markov-chain-monte-carlo.html) replaces them with states from a [Markov chain](markov-chains.qmd) designed to have the posterior as its stationary distribution.

## Define the target before the chain

Suppose $\Theta$ is a standardized articulation-rate contrast. After specifying a likelihood and prior, the inferential target is

$$
p(\theta\mid\mathbf{y}).
$$

For a function $g$, the posterior quantity of interest is

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\Theta)\mid\mathbf{y}]
=
\int g(\theta)p(\theta\mid\mathbf{y})\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

MCMC does not define this posterior. It constructs a dependent sequence

$$
\theta^{(1)},\theta^{(2)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}
$$

whose long-run distribution is intended to be $p(\theta\mid\mathbf{y})$.

## Use chain averages

Once the chain has reached and explored its stationary distribution, approximate $I$ with

$$
\widehat{I}_S
=
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\theta^{(s)}).
$$

The formula resembles ordinary Monte Carlo integration. The difference is that adjacent MCMC states are dependent.

A chain can still support consistent averages when its transition rule preserves the target and is ergodic. In the finite state case, the irreducibility and aperiodicity conditions from the preceding page are sufficient for this behavior. Dependence changes efficiency rather than automatically invalidating the average.

## Examine a chain with a known target

Consider the transition

$$
\Theta^{(s+1)}
=
\mu
+\rho(\Theta^{(s)}-\mu)
+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\varepsilon_s,
$$

where $\varepsilon_s\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,1)$ and $|\rho|<1$. Its stationary distribution is $\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,1)$.

Set $\mu=.40$ and $\rho=.90$. Starting at $-4$ produces a chain that initially moves toward the target region and then continues to explore it.

```{r}
#| label: known-target-markov-chain
#| echo: true

set.seed(183)
draw_count <- 20000
mu <- .40
rho <- .90
theta <- numeric(draw_count)
theta[1] <- -4

for (s in 2:draw_count) {
  theta[s] <- mu + rho * (theta[s - 1] - mu) +
    sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(1)
}

saved <- theta[1001:draw_count]
stopifnot(abs(mean(saved) - mu) < .05)
stopifnot(abs(sd(saved) - 1) < .05)
c(mean = mean(saved), sd = sd(saved))
```

The first 1,000 states are omitted here only because the chain was deliberately initialized far from its stationary region. Discarding early iterations does not repair a transition that cannot reach part of the target.

Multiple chains should begin from different plausible initial values. If they move toward and then repeatedly explore the same region, initialization appears to have lost its influence. If they remain separated, averaging them hides the failure.

The omitted initialization period is commonly called warmup. In adaptive samplers, warmup also tunes the transition algorithm. Those adaptation states are not included in posterior summaries.

## Keep three distributions separate

| object | role |
|---|---|
| posterior target | distribution the analysis seeks to approximate |
| transition distribution | conditional rule for moving to a new state |
| empirical draw distribution | finite collection of states produced by one run |

The transition distribution is not the posterior. It is designed so that repeated transitions preserve the posterior. The finite empirical distribution is not exactly the posterior either. It approximates the target with Monte Carlo error.

## Distinguish posterior spread from chain behavior

A wide posterior may reflect limited linguistic information under the model. A slowly moving chain reflects computational inefficiency. Collecting more data can change posterior spread. Running the chain longer can reduce Monte Carlo error, but it does not add linguistic evidence.

A long run does not prove that a chain has explored the target distribution correctly. A chain can repeat the wrong region for millions of steps. Diagnostics later assess whether multiple chains agree and whether dependence leaves enough effective information.

MCMC output should thus be treated as an approximation with an audit trail. The model defines the target, the algorithm generates dependent draws, and diagnostics assess the finite run.

1. Which distribution is the inferential target in MCMC?
2. Why are adjacent chain states generally not independent?
3. What must a transition rule accomplish before chain averages approximate posterior expectations?
4. Why can increasing the number of iterations reduce Monte Carlo error without narrowing the posterior?
